title: CORNER Competitive Battle Cards
summary: One-page battle cards for every competitor type Patrik might face in a sales call. Pull up the right card, know exactly what to say. Covers DIY tools, fractional CAIOs, chatbot vendors, AI consulting agencies, and construction-specific competitors.
content:
CORNER Competitive Battle Cards

Author: Steve (AI Advisory Lead) Date: 2026-03-16 For: Patrik (sales calls), Ash (follow-up conversations), Jacob (email objection handling) How to use: When a prospect mentions a competitor or alternative, pull up the matching card. Each card is self-contained: what they are, where they're weak, what to say.

Card 1: "I'm already using ChatGPT"

What they think they have: An AI tool that answers questions.

What they actually have: A single-purpose text box with no memory of their business, no connection to their tools, no ability to act. They type a question, get an answer, copy-paste it somewhere, and do the work themselves. Every conversation starts from zero.

Where they're weak:

  • No memory between sessions (unless they manually re-explain their business every time)
  • Cannot take action (can't send emails, update calendars, manage tasks, follow up with clients)
  • One tool, not a team. Cannot hand off work between specialties.
  • No context about the prospect's business operations, clients, or history
  • Requires the business owner to know what to ask. Most don't.
  • No QA. No oversight. No pipeline. Just raw output.

What to say: "ChatGPT is a great tool. We use it too. But there's a difference between having a tool and having a team. ChatGPT answers one question at a time. Corner gives you six agents working in parallel: one manages your schedule, one handles client follow-up, one tracks your pipeline, one does your outreach, one creates content, and one checks everyone else's work. They remember your business, they talk to each other, and they work while you sleep. ChatGPT doesn't do that."

The closer: "Most business owners try ChatGPT for two weeks and stop. Not because it's bad, because they don't know what to ask, and it doesn't plug into their operations. Corner plugs in on day one."

Card 2: "I use Zapier / Make / n8n"

What they think they have: Automation that connects their tools.

What they actually have: Trigger-action sequences that break when anything changes. If-this-then-that logic. No reasoning, no judgment, no adaptation. When a workflow breaks, nobody notices until a client complains.

Where they're weak:

  • Brittle. One field changes in a form and the whole workflow dies silently.
  • No intelligence. Zapier connects apps. It doesn't understand context.
  • Requires technical setup. Most small business owners abandon it within a month.
  • Can't handle ambiguity. "Schedule this call sometime next week" breaks automation. An agent handles it.
  • No visual interface. It's a backend tool. Invisible until something goes wrong.
  • Per-task pricing adds up. Heavy users pay $200-500/month for Zapier alone and still need to build everything themselves.

What to say: "Zapier connects apps. Corner runs operations. Here's the difference: Zapier can connect your calendar to your email. Corner can read a new project request, check your crew's availability, draft a response to the client, schedule the site visit, create the estimate, and update your project tracker. Without you touching anything. And when something unexpected happens, Corner reasons through it instead of crashing."

The closer: "You shouldn't have to be a programmer to automate your business. That's our job."

Card 3: "We hired a fractional Chief AI Officer"

What they think they have: A senior AI strategist guiding their business.

What they actually have: An expensive advisor who sells hours, not outcomes. $2,500-$30,000/month for someone's time. They'll write you a roadmap. They won't build the system. They won't run it. They won't maintain it.

Where they're weak:

  • Sell time, not systems. When they leave, nothing stays.
  • Can't scale. One person, limited hours. Your operations don't stop at 5 PM.
  • No platform. No dashboard. No ongoing automation. Just meetings and documents.
  • Expensive for what you get. $10k/month for 20 hours of advisory. Corner gives you 24/7 operations for $3k/month.
  • They advise. You still have to execute everything yourself or hire someone to build it.
  • No QA. No monitoring. No self-healing. They hand you a plan and move on.

What to say: "A fractional CAIO gives you advice. Corner gives you action. For $3k/month, you get a team of AI agents that actually runs your operations, not a consultant who tells you what you should do and leaves you to figure out the how. And Corner doesn't bill by the hour. It works 24/7, 365."

The closer: "If you've been paying for AI advice but nothing's changed in your operations, that's the gap Corner fills. We don't advise. We build and run."

Card 4: "We're looking at [Intercom AI / Drift / a chatbot]"

What they think they have: An AI solution for customer communication.

What they actually have: A customer-facing chatbot. It handles inbound questions from website visitors. That's it. One channel, one function, customer-facing only. Nothing for internal operations.

Where they're weak:

  • Customer-facing only. Does nothing for scheduling, estimating, invoicing, internal comms, task management.
  • One bot, not a team. Can't hand off work. Can't coordinate across functions.
  • Doesn't know your business deeply. Trained on your FAQ, not your operations.
  • Doesn't learn or improve over time in meaningful operational ways.
  • Expensive for what it is. Intercom AI is $29-132/seat/month. For a 10-person company, that's $300-$1,300/month for a chatbot. Corner is $3k/month for an entire AI operations team.

What to say: "Chatbots handle customer questions. Corner handles your business. A chatbot answers 'what are your hours?' Corner schedules the appointment, assigns the crew, sends the confirmation, follows up the next day, and invoices the client. A chatbot is one tool. Corner is your back office."

The closer: "We're not replacing your chatbot. We're handling everything your chatbot can't."

Card 5: "We talked to [AI consulting firm / Estes Media / Authority AI]"

What they think they have: A professional firm that'll build them an AI solution.

What they actually have: A project engagement. They'll scope it, build it, hand it off, and invoice. When something breaks, you call them again and pay again. No ongoing management. No living system.

Where they're weak:

  • Project-based, not platform-based. They build and leave.
  • No managed operations. When the project ends, you're on your own.
  • No visual interface. You get custom code or configured tools, not a dashboard you enjoy using.
  • Expensive per engagement. $10k-$50k per project. That's the build cost alone, with no ongoing management.
  • No proof they run it themselves. They're selling consulting, not a system they use daily.
  • When AI tools change (and they change fast), your custom build breaks. Who maintains it?

What to say: "Most AI firms sell you a project. We sell you a team. Here's the difference: they'll spend 6 weeks building you something, hand it over, and move on to the next client. When something changes, and with AI things change every month, you call them back and pay again. Corner is a living platform. We update it continuously. Your agents get smarter over time. We manage everything. And we built this system for our own business first. We run on it every day. That's the proof."

The closer: "Ask them to show you their own company running on the system they're selling you. We can."

Card 6: "I can just hire someone to do this"

What they think they have: A hiring option that gives them a real person.

What they actually have: A $4,000-$6,000/month expense (fully loaded) for one person who works 40 hours, calls in sick, takes vacations, needs training, might leave, and can only do one thing at a time.

Where they're weak:

  • One person = one function. A bookkeeper doesn't do scheduling. A scheduler doesn't do outreach.
  • $4-6k/month fully loaded. Benefits, taxes, equipment, management overhead.
  • Training time. 2-4 weeks before they're productive. Corner is productive on day one.
  • Turnover risk. Average admin turnover is 12-18 months. Then you start over.
  • Limited hours. They stop at 5 PM. Your clients don't.
  • Single point of failure. They're sick? Everything stops.

What to say: "I get it. Real people are great. But let me put it in numbers. One admin hire costs you $4,000 to $6,000 a month, fully loaded. They work 40 hours. They handle one job. Corner costs $3,000 a month, works 24/7, and gives you a team: scheduling, follow-up, estimating support, outreach, content, and quality control. All of that. For less than one part-time person."

The closer: "You'll still hire people as you grow. But hire them for the work that needs a human. Let Corner handle the rest."

Card 7: "We don't need AI" / "AI isn't ready"

What they think: AI is overhyped, unreliable, or irrelevant to their industry.

What's actually happening: They've seen bad AI demos, or they tried ChatGPT once and it hallucinated. They're judging the category by the worst examples.

Where this thinking fails:

  • AI is already being used by their competitors (even if they don't know it)
  • The "AI isn't ready" window is closing. By the time they decide it's ready, early adopters have a 2-year head start.
  • They're spending 15-20 hours/week on admin work that AI handles right now. That's $1,000-$2,000/week in their time.
  • "We don't need AI" usually means "I don't understand what it can do for my specific business."

What to say: "I hear that a lot. And honestly, most AI demos are terrible. They show you a chatbot that gets confused. That's not what we do. Let me ask you this: how many hours a week do you spend on scheduling, follow-ups, and paperwork? [Let them answer.] OK. What if half of that just... happened? Automatically. Correctly. Every day. That's what we built. I can show you in 20 minutes."

The closer: "You don't have to believe in AI. You have to believe in getting 10 hours of your week back. The AI part is our problem."

Card 8: "That's too expensive" / "We can't afford $3k/month"

What they think: $3,000/month is a lot of money.

What's actually true: $3,000/month is $140/business day. If Corner saves them 2 hours/day of admin work, and their time is worth $100/hour, that's $200/day in value for $140. Positive ROI on day one.

What to say: "I hear you. $3k/month is real money. Let me show you the math. [Open ROI calculator.] You said you spend about [X] hours a week on admin. At your billing rate, that's [Y] per week in time. Corner costs $140 a business day. If it saves you even two hours a day, you're ahead. And that's before counting the jobs you win because your follow-up is faster, your estimates go out same-day, and no lead falls through the cracks."

If they genuinely can't afford it: "Totally understand. Here's what I'd suggest: we do a one-time operations audit. $2,500 flat. We spend two weeks understanding your business, identify exactly where AI saves you time, and deliver a written report. If the numbers make sense, we build from there. If not, you've still got a useful operational analysis. No ongoing commitment."

Never discount. The $2,500 audit is the floor. If they can't afford the audit, they're not the right client.

How to Use These Cards

  1. Before a discovery call: Read Card 7 and Card 8. Most calls start with skepticism or price resistance.
  2. During a demo: If they mention a specific tool or competitor, pull up that card.
  3. In follow-up emails: Use the "What to say" language adapted for written form. Keep it brief.
  4. For Jacob's cold email replies: When a prospect responds with "we already use [X]," pull the card and draft a response.

The goal is never to trash the competitor. It's to show the gap. Corner does things none of these alternatives can do. Lead with what Corner adds, not what they lack.

Every objection is a buying signal. They're engaging, not dismissing. Use these cards to turn engagement into action.
